To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the contraction times of human muscle fibres can be determined from the contraction time of twitches evoked electrically and that the contraction times can be correlated with the histochemical properties of the fibres.
the contraction times of human muscle fibres can be studied by recording twitches in situ in bundles of fibres and that the contraction times agree with histochemical findings.
the mean contraction time of motor unit twitches, as recorded by needle electrodes, is a good index of the fibre composition of the motor units.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relation between the contraction time and fibre type in the intact human muscle.
the relationship between contraction time and fibre type in intact human muscles, with a comparison of the contraction time of voluntarily and electrically activated motor units.
the relation between histochemistry and the mechanical properties of intact muscle fibres.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the contraction times of the human muscle are related to the fibre types and that the fibre types can be identified by the histochemical method of Gomori and by the contraction time of twitches.
the time to peak contraction of a twitch is a good indicator of the proportion of fibrous and non-fibrous material in a bundle of muscle fibres.
the contraction times of human muscle are related to fibre type and to the temperature.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are three types of muscle fibres in humans, the type with the shortest contraction times, the fastest twitching, being the type with the lowest oxidative capacity.
the contraction time of a motor unit is mainly determined by the type of fibres it contains, the temperature coefficient being higher for fibres rich in myoglobin and mitochondria.

the contraction times of the motor unit fibres in intact muscles of normal humans correspond to the histochemical findings, and that the contraction time is a useful parameter for the study of the functional organization of the motor system.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the contraction times of human motor units are in agreement with the histochemical fibre types, that the contraction time of a voluntary motor unit is not significantly different from that of a twitch elicited by electrical stimuli, and that the force of fasciculating motor units is about three times that evoked by electrical stimuli.

the time to peak contraction of bundles of fibres is a reliable index of fibre type in intact muscle, and that the contraction time of motor unit action potentials is not an adequate index of fibre type.
we can use this technique to study the effects of drugs and other interventions on muscle contractility in humans.
